newsitem.title: INDONESIA: FOCUS-Rupiah seen weakening further in short term.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Rupiah seen weakening further in short term.

text.p: The Indonesian rupiah, which has been volatile after plunging to a record low against the dollar on Monday, is likely to weaken in the short-term despite the country's strong economic fundamentals, economists said on Thursday.
They said problems in rolling over corporate debt and contagion from weakness in several regional currencies should push the rupiah toward the lower end of the central bank's intervention band.
"I still think we are still firmly in an environment of dollar strength against the regionals," said Desmond Supple, regional currency specialist at BZW Asia in Singapore.

"Over the short-term, I would expect to see convergence of spot rupiah and the weaker end of the intervention band. While fundamentally this weakness is not justified, this contagion continues to ensure that the perceptions of fundamentals are more important than the fundamentals themselves."
The rupiah opened in Jakarta at 2,575/85 against the dollar on Thursday and by late evening was trading at 2,613 in the spot market. The central bank posted its intervention band at 2,378/2,682.
It crashed to a historic low of 2,665 against the dollar on Monday after becoming the latest currency to fall victim to speculative attacks which have plagued the region.
Central bank intervention brought about a partial recovery on that day, but the currency has been extremely volatile with swings between 2,530 and 2,625 since then.
Traders say although the rate has not fallen out of the band, Bank Indonesia, the central bank, has pumped some $700 million into the market.
But they add that regional fallout, especially from the Thai baht, has made those efforts apparently futile.
UBS Research said in a report that markets would take some time to assess the differences between the fundamentals of the Indonesian and Thai economies.
"The baht was attacked because of the perception that the rigid exchange rate regime was inconsistent with sharply dropping economic activity and high domestic interest rates," it said.
"Conditions are different in Indonesia, which has a much more flexible foreign exchange system, robust economic activity and ample liquidity in the financial system."
But the report cautioned that rupiah weakness would persist for the next three to six months, at least partly because of problems in Indonesian corporate debt.

"There is evidence that more Indonesian corporates are facing difficulties in rolling over their maturing foreign liabilities," UBS said, pointing to higher risk premiums and possibly lower credit limits because of falling investor confidence in nations with large current account deficits.

"As a result, more Indonesian corporates will have to buy rupiah and convert into foreign currency domestically," it said. "Unless supported by strong intervention from Bank Indonesia, this will add pressure to the rupiah."
Over the longer-term, analysts and dealers said 2,550 was fair value for the rupiah.
"At the 2,550 level, that's really comfortable," said an analyst with a U.S. bank in Singapore, adding that many fund managers were looking to sell dollars above the 2,600 level.
Others said the longer-term view was that strong exports in the second half of the year should bolster the currency, which would then recover to a four-to-five percent guided depreciation trend.
